question.problem:
Suppose the following data is sampled from a population. Compute an unbiased estimate of the population variance.

$$
13,\,15,\,9,\,11,\,12
$$
question.worked_solution:
Suppose ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…{X}_{n}$ is a sequence of random variables representing a random sample of size $n$ drawn from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population variance ${\sigma }^{2}.$ Then, the sample variance ${S}^{2}$ is given by

$$
{S}^{2}=\frac{1}{n-1}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{({X}_{i}-\overset{―}{X})}^{2}=\frac{n}{n-1}[\overset{―}{{X}^{2}}-{(\overset{―}{X})}^{2}].
$$

Note that:

- $\overset{―}{X}$ is the sample mean,

- the sample variance ${S}^{2}$ is an unbiased estimator of the population variance ${\sigma }^{2},$ and

- ${\overset{^}{\sigma }}^{2}={s}^{2}$ denotes the unbiased estimate of ${\sigma }^{2}$ computed from the sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}.$

First, we will compute the quantity

$$
\overset{―}{{x}^{2}}-{(\overset{―}{x})}^{2}.
$$

We proceed as follows:

- The mean of the data is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{x} & =\frac{1}{5}(13+15+9+11+12) \\  & =\frac{60}{5} \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

- The mean of the squared data is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{{x}^{2}} & =\frac{1}{5}({13}^{2}+{15}^{2}+{9}^{2}+{11}^{2}+{12}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{740}{5} \\  & =148.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{{x}^{2}}-{(\overset{―}{x})}^{2} & =148-{12}^{2} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the sample variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\overset{^}{\sigma }}^{2} & ={s}^{2} \\  & =\frac{n}{n-1}[\overset{―}{{x}^{2}}-{(\overset{―}{x})}^{2}] \\  & =\frac{5}{5-1}\cdot 4 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, an unbiased estimate of the population variance is $5.$
